About this simulation

On screen
Left: white dwarf 1 (born at 5 × 107 K) and white dwarf 2 on a night sky with the Earth between them, all three drawn at the same true scale (radius 0.0125 R☉, 1.36 Earth radii). Each disc has the blackbody colour of its surface temperature, and its glow grows with log L. Right: L against t on logarithmic axes, 104 to 1011 yr across and 10−5 to 10 L☉ upwards, with a legend. Each curve is traced up to the current age with a dot at its end, and a dotted line marks the age of the Universe. From card 4 the cooling time t0 of each star is ticked on the age axis; the dashed late-time line L ∝ t−7/5 appears once the age passes 2.2 × 109 yr.
Controls
The birth core temperature of white dwarf 2, 5 × 107 to 3 × 108 K (white dwarf 1 stays at 5 × 107 K). The age slider is logarithmic, 104 to 1.4 × 1010 yr, with chips for round ages; touching it pauses play. ▶ Play advances the age by one decade every 4 s and stops at 1.4 × 1010 yr.
Readouts
In the sidebar: the age t; L1 and L2 in solar luminosities and their ratio L2/L1; each star's cooling time t0 (from card 4); and each surface temperature Teff.
Model
Mestel cooling of 0.6 M☉ carbon white dwarfs. The ion core has one uniform temperature Tc and stores U = (3/2)(M/Amu)kBTc; the heat leaks through a thin envelope of Kramers opacity, L = C M Tc7/2 with C = 6.6 × 10−3 W K−7/2 (M in M☉), at fixed radius. Then L = L0(1 + t/t0)−7/5 with t0 = (2/5)U0/L0 ∝ T0−5/2. Left out: neutrino cooling (important for young, hot white dwarfs), crystallisation and the drop in heat capacity of a cold crystal (important below about 10−4 L☉), and the life of the parent star. The ages are therefore rough: full cooling models put the oldest disc white dwarfs at about 8–10 × 109 yr.

Guided Inquiry

1 · The early years

Set the core temperature at birth of white dwarf 2 to 2 × 108 K and the age to 104 years. Before pressing play and letting the age run to 106 years, predict what happens to the luminosity of white dwarf 1 over that time.

2 · Comparing the two luminosities

Keep the settings of question 1 and return the age to 104 years. White dwarf 2 has a core four times hotter than white dwarf 1. Before reading the readouts, predict the ratio of their luminosities L2/L1.

3 · Which curve bends first

Keep the core temperature of white dwarf 2 at 2 × 108 K and the age at 104 years. Before pressing play and letting the age run to 109 years, predict which curve on the luminosity graph bends down first.

4 · After ten billion years

Keep the core temperature of white dwarf 2 at 2 × 108 K. Before moving the age to 1010 years (the 1010 chip under the age slider), predict the ratio L2/L1 you will read there.

5 · A hotter birth

Keep the age at 1010 years. Before moving the core temperature at birth of white dwarf 2 from 2 × 108 K up to 3 × 108 K, predict what happens to L2.

6 · The faintest white dwarfs

Keep the core temperature of white dwarf 2 at 3 × 108 K and the age at 1010 years. Surveys find almost no white dwarfs in the disc of the Galaxy fainter than a few times 10−5 L☉. Before reading the luminosities, predict what this cutoff tells us.

7 · What the curves say

A white dwarf has no fusion. It leaks the heat stored in its ions through a thin, opaque surface layer, with L ∝ Tc7/2, and it does not contract, so it only cools.

Each star stays near its birth luminosity until t ≈ t0 ∝ T0−5/2, so the hotter-born star fades first. After that every curve joins one line, L ∝ t−7/5, whatever the birth temperature.

So a white dwarf's luminosity is a clock, and the faintest white dwarfs in the disc give its age, about 1010 years. This is the simple Mestel model: neutrino cooling, crystallisation and the parent star's life are left out.

The Physics

How a White Dwarf Fades · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

Two white dwarfs of the same mass start with different core temperatures and then cool. This sim sets them side by side on the sky, graphs how their light changes with age, and lets you set how hot the second one is born and how old both are.

What you'll learn

  • Where the heat of a white dwarf is stored and how it leaks out.
  • The cooling time t0 and the law that gives L at any age.
  • How two stars of different birth temperature compare as they age.
  • What the faintest white dwarfs tell us about the Galaxy's disc.
The sim's two views as they open, before anything is traced: three discs at one scale, and the empty graph.

What's on screen

  • White dwarf 1, born at 5×107 K, and white dwarf 2, born at a temperature you set, with the Earth between them. Both are 0.6 M☉ of carbon, drawn at one scale.
  • Graph of luminosity L (in L☉) against age t (in years), both on logarithmic axes, with a dotted line at the sim's age of the Universe, 1.4×1010 yr.
  • Readouts give the age, both luminosities and their ratio, the cooling time t0 and the surface temperature Teff of each star.
See itLook at the opening view. Watch for: the two white dwarfs and the Earth on the sky, and the readouts at an age of 104 yr.

Fixed: both stars are 0.6 M☉ of carbon (A = 12), with CL = 6.6×10−3 W K−7/2 per M☉ and a radius of 0.0125 R☉, which is 1.36 Earth radii.

03

Heat store and leak: the nuclei hold the heat, a thin envelope lets it out

A white dwarf has no fusion. Its electrons are degenerate and cannot give up their kinetic energy, so the heat that is lost is the thermal energy of the nuclei, which form an ideal gas. For nuclei of mass number A at temperature Tc (notes, eq. 5.15):

Equation (5.15). mu is the atomic mass unit and kB is Boltzmann's constant.

The interior is at nearly one temperature, because degenerate electrons conduct heat well, as the electrons in a metal do. The heat escapes by radiative diffusion through a thin surface layer in which the electrons are not degenerate. With the Kramers opacity (§4.3), the luminosity is (eq. 5.16):

Equation (5.16). CL depends on the composition of the surface layer.
Sketch of the model, not to scale: a core at one temperature Tc under a thin envelope.

In the sim, M is in M☉ and CL = 6.6×10−3 W K−7/2. At Tc = 5×107 K, a 0.6 M☉ carbon core stores U = 6.2×1040 J.

Key idea. The radius is held by the degeneracy pressure of the electrons, not by the temperature, so cooling does not shrink the star. Both discs stay at 1.36 Earth radii, and only Tc changes the leak.
04

The cooling time t0 sets when the fading starts, and L = L0(1 + t/t0)−7/5

The luminosity is the rate at which U falls, dU/dt = −L, which gives (eq. 5.17):

Equation (5.17), from dU/dt = −L with U from (5.15) and L from (5.16).

The mass cancels. Separating the variables and integrating Tc−7/2dTc from T0 gives Tc−5/2 − T0−5/2 = (t/t0)T0−5/2, with the cooling time (eq. 5.18):

Equation (5.18). U0 and L0 are the thermal energy and the luminosity at t = 0.

Since L goes as Tc7/2, the luminosity is (eq. 5.19):

Equation (5.19), the law the sim draws.

While t is much smaller than t0 the bracket is close to 1 and L stays near L0. The age at which the star starts to fade is t0, and t0 is proportional to T0−5/2, so a hotter star has a shorter clock.

In the sim, white dwarf 1 has t0 = 2.25×108 yr and L0 = 9.14×10−3 L☉. At 2×108 K, four times hotter, white dwarf 2 has L0 = 1.17 L☉, which is 47/2 = 128 times more, and t0 = 7.02×106 yr, which is 45/2 = 32 times shorter.

05

Two curves, one line: the hotter star bends first, then both fall together

L against t for the two white dwarfs at the sim's opening T0,2 = 2×108 K, from its own formula. The ticks mark each t0.

Each curve is flat until t reaches its own t0. White dwarf 2 bends first because its t0 is 32 times shorter, and it keeps falling faster. Its lead over white dwarf 1 shrinks from 127.75 at 104 yr to 4.73 at 108 yr, 1.32 at 109 yr and 1.03 at 1010 yr.

For t much larger than t0, eq. 5.19 becomes L ≈ L0(t/t0)−7/5. Here L0 goes as T07/2 and t07/5 as T0−7/2, so L0t07/5 does not depend on T0. Every curve of this mass and composition joins one line, L ∝ t−7/5, the dashed straight line of Figure 72.

At 1010 yr the sim reads L1 = 4.36×10−5 L☉ and L2 = 4.49×10−5 L☉, with surface temperatures of 4 195 K and 4 227 K.

See itMove the age to 109 yr. Watch for: the ratio down to 1.32, with L1 at 8.51×10−4 L☉ and L2 at 1.12×10−3 L☉.
See itNow take the age to 1010 yr. Watch for: the curves almost on top of each other, the ratio at 1.03 and the two surface temperatures both close to 4 200 K.
Key idea. The light of an old white dwarf no longer remembers the temperature it was born at.
06

A hotter birth changes almost nothing at ten billion years

Late in life, L depends on the birth temperature only through the small offset between t and t + t0. White dwarf 2 gets hotter at birth, so its t0 gets shorter and its L0 larger, in just the proportions that cancel.

Take T0,2 from 2×108 K to 3×108 K. At birth, L0 rises from 1.17 to 4.84 L☉, by (3/2)7/2 = 4.1, and t0 falls from 7.02×106 to 2.55×106 yr. At an age of 1010 yr, L2 goes from 4.494×10−5 to 4.497×10−5 L☉, a change of 0.06 per cent.

L at birth and at an age of 1010 yr against the birth temperature of a 0.6 M☉ white dwarf, from the sim's formula.
See itSet T0,2 = 3×108 K and the age to 1010 yr. Watch for: L2 reading 4.50×10−5 L☉, about the same as at 2×108 K, and t0 of white dwarf 2 down to 2.55×106 yr.
Key idea. The luminosity of a very old white dwarf is a clock that does not depend on how the star started.
07

The faintest white dwarfs date the disc of the Galaxy

After a time long compared with t0, the age of a white dwarf is (notes, p. 207):

The age from the luminosity, for t much larger than t0, independent of the initial temperature.

In this model (2/5)U/L equals t + t0 exactly, so for old stars it is the age whatever the birth temperature. Measuring L and Tc therefore gives an age without knowing how hot the star began.

The faintest white dwarfs in the disc have cooling ages of about 1010 yr, and the number observed at each luminosity falls sharply below the luminosity of the faintest. No white dwarf in the disc has had time to cool further, so the cutoff gives an age for the disc, which can be compared with the ages of the oldest star clusters (§4.8).

In the sim, white dwarfs of this mass reach 4.5×10−5 L☉ at 1010 yr and 2.8×10−5 L☉ at the end of the run, 1.4×1010 yr.

See itRun the age to the end, 1.4×1010 yr, with T0,2 = 3×108 K. Watch for: L1 = 2.75×10−5 L☉ and L2 = 2.81×10−5 L☉, the surface temperatures near 3 700 K.
08

Where it matters

  • A clock for the Galaxy. The luminosity cutoff of the faintest white dwarfs gives an age for the disc, to compare with the oldest star clusters.
  • No dependence on the start. The age comes from L alone, so it holds for white dwarfs of unknown birth temperature.
  • Degeneracy at work. The electrons conduct heat and fix the radius, while the nuclei carry the heat.
Go deeper: what the sim leaves out
  • Neutrino cooling, which matters for young, hot white dwarfs, is left out.
  • Crystallisation and the drop in heat capacity of a cold crystal, which matter below about 10−4 L☉, are left out, and so is the life of the parent star. The sim says its ages are therefore rough.
  • Its dotted line at 1.4×1010 yr is the sim's age of the Universe, and the run stops there.
09

Summary

In one line. A white dwarf has no fusion: it leaks the heat stored in its nuclei through a thin envelope, and its cooling time t0 is the time scale of that loss.

Key points

  • U = (3/2)(M/Amu)kBTc and L = CLMTc7/2 give L = L0(1 + t/t0)−7/5.
  • t0 = (2/5)U0/L0 goes as T0−5/2.
  • Late on, L ∝ t−7/5 and t ≈ (2/5)U/L, for every birth temperature.

Common mix-ups

  • "The luminosity falls by the same factor in every decade, from the start." It is flat while t is much smaller than t0.
  • "Four times the core temperature means four times the luminosity." L ∝ Tc7/2, so the factor is 128.
  • "The star born hotter keeps its lead." It joins the same t−7/5 line.
  • "A white dwarf shrinks as it cools, like an ordinary gas." Degenerate electrons hold the radius.

Things to try on your own

  • Set T0,2 = 5×107 K. Predict L2/L1 at every age, then check it (exactly 1).
  • Set T0,2 = 108 K at age 104 yr. Predict the ratio from 27/2 (11.31) and t0 (3.97×107 yr).
